claims.verbatim_text:
Under suboptimal average temperatures and night 
temperatures, the relative growth rate for tomato 
plants is reduced because of thicker leaves (re-
duced specific leaf area, SLA). Photosynthesis is 
not affected by suboptimal night temperature 
(Fig. 7.13).
claims.claim_statement: Suboptimal night temperature reduces tomato relative growth rate (via thicker leaves / lower SLA) while leaving photosynthesis unaffected.
claims.subject: suboptimal night temperature
claims.relation: reduces relative growth rate without reducing
claims.object: tomato whole-plant growth rate (photosynthesis unchanged)

scope.conditions: suboptimal average and night temperature, greenhouse/climate-cabinet

claims.why: It is the exact C2 premise: cool nights limit growth (sink) while carbon supply (photosynthesis) is unimpaired, which is the source-sink imbalance the hypothesis needs.

claims.verbatim_text:
Suppression of the shoot growth 
rates and leaf area expansion under subopti-
mal temperatures (e.g. 17/14°C compared with 
22/18°C) was related to hormonal signaling 
(ABA, auxin), rather than a restriction in the 
rates of net CO2 assimilation (Ntatsi et al., 2013).
claims.claim_statement: Shoot growth and leaf expansion suppression at 17/14 degC versus 22/18 degC day/night was attributed to hormonal signalling (ABA, auxin) rather than to restricted net CO2 assimilation.
claims.subject: suboptimal day/night temperature (17/14 vs 22/18 degC)
claims.relation: suppresses via hormonal signalling rather than assimilation limitation
claims.object: shoot growth rate and leaf area expansion

scope.conditions: 17/14 degC vs 22/18 degC day/night

claims.why: It confirms C2 (cool nights limit growth) and localises the limitation to the sink/signalling side, not the carbon-supply side, which is what C3 requires for carbon to be left over.

claims.verbatim_text:
As tomato is a tropical species, no growth occurs 
below 12°C, and long-term exposure to these 
low temperatures causes chilling injury.
claims.claim_statement: Tomato growth ceases entirely below 12 degC.
claims.subject: temperature below 12 degC
claims.object: tomato growth

scope.conditions: temperature < 12 degC

claims.why: It fixes a hard lower threshold at which structural growth (the hexose sink) stops, defining the night-temperature regime under which C2 would be strongest.

claims.verbatim_text:
a reduced demand for photo-assimilates 
due to reduction or cessation of growth and de-
velopment
claims.claim_statement: Low temperature reduces the demand for photo-assimilates because growth and development slow or stop.
claims.subject: low temperature (with high irradiance, early spring)
claims.object: photo-assimilates, via reduced or arrested growth and development

scope.conditions: high irradiance with low temperature (early spring)

claims.why: This is the explicit statement that cold reduces assimilate demand, the C2->C3 bridge: unconsumed assimilate is what the hypothesis claims remains as hexose.

claims.section: Ch. 7 Tomato - Day and night temperature
claims.verbatim_text:
For a mature crop, the 
long-term average temperature rather than the 
day-night temperature regime determines crop 
growth and yield. Temperature integration up 
to 24 days (amplitude 3 or 6°C) did not influence 
yield (De Koning, 1990).
claims.claim_statement: For a mature tomato crop, long-term average temperature rather than the day/night temperature regime determines growth and yield, and temperature integration over up to 24 days did not change yield.
claims.subject: day-night temperature regime (as distinct from 24-h mean)
claims.object: crop growth and yield of a mature tomato crop

scope.conditions: mature greenhouse crop, temperature integration amplitude 3 or 6 degC over up to 24 days

quantitative.magnitude_text: Temperature integration up to 24 days (amplitude 3 or 6°C) did not influence yield

claims.why: If a mature crop integrates temperature over many days, a single cool night should not create a distinct next-morning carbon state, which is what the hypothesis requires.

claims.verbatim_text:
Reduction in length growth resulting from 
a so-called negative DIF (difference between day 
and night temperature) has been reported by 
many authors and for a large variety of crops 
including tomato (Fig. 7.2).
claims.claim_statement: A negative DIF (night temperature higher than day temperature) reduces stem length growth across many crops including tomato, so at equal 24-h mean a cooler night is associated with MORE elongation growth.
claims.subject: negative DIF (night warmer than day)
claims.object: stem length growth

scope.species: many crops incl. Solanum lycopersicum; Fig. 7.2 compares 26/16 vs 16/26 degC day/night
scope.conditions: equal 24-h mean temperature, differing DIF
scope.timescale: weeks (8 weeks after sowing in Fig. 7.2)

claims.why: DIF experiments show that at constant 24-h mean a COOL night gives greater elongation growth, the opposite of the assumption that a cool night suppresses the structural sink.

claims.verbatim_text:
Bours (2014) con-
cluded that negative DIF affects growth by directly 
affecting the phase and amplitude of circadian 
clock genes, which in turn control downstream 
processes such as starch metabolism and hor-
mone signaling pathways.
claims.claim_statement: Day/night temperature differential is proposed to act on growth by shifting circadian clock gene phase and amplitude, which then control starch metabolism and hormone signalling.
claims.subject: negative DIF
claims.relation: acts on growth through phase/amplitude changes in circadian clock genes controlling
claims.object: starch metabolism and hormone signalling

scope.species: not specified in this sentence (crop/Arabidopsis literature)
scope.conditions: differing day-night temperature regimes

claims.why: It offers a competing route from night temperature to leaf carbohydrate status - clock retiming of starch turnover - that does not require failed structural conversion.

claims.section: Ch. 5.3 Effect of temperature on biomass allocation
claims.verbatim_text:
Temperature affects sink strength of plant 
organs directly (Walker and Ho, 1977; Williams and Marinos, 1977; Yoshioka et al.,

claims.section: Ch. 5.3 Effect of temperature on biomass allocation - Abstract
claims.verbatim_text:
It is concluded that dry matter distribution in tomato is not significantly affected by 
temperature directly, which means that the temperature effect (18-24°C) on the 
generative sink strength is not much different from the temperature effect on the 
vegetative sink strength.

claims.object: dry matter partitioning between fruits and vegetative parts

claims.why: It is a null on partitioning, not on absolute sink activity - it bounds C2 by showing 18-24 degC does not redirect carbon between organs, only scales all sinks together.

claims.section: General introduction - growth and maintenance respiration
claims.verbatim_text:
The growth coefficient (mg CO2 g'1 dry mass synthesised) is

On

and less

다른 연구결과에 따르면, 애기장대는 5°C

OUT-OF-ASSIGNMENT SOURCE. 857 is NOT one of my nine assigned papers. It was found by a corpus-wide regex sweep for 'night temperature' within 250 characters of a carbohydrate term, which returned only 1246 and the 857/1276 duplicate pair across all 1,281 documents. I read the relevant sections of 857 (model overview, section 4.2.2, Appendix C, Table 3) before citing them.

THE DECISIVE MEASUREMENT IS ABSENT FROM MY SET. No paper I read measures dawn or pre-dawn leaf HEXOSE as a function of NIGHT TEMPERATURE. The two components exist separately but never together: (a) 1027 measures leaf mono-/disaccharides and starch at the end of the night period, deliberately and for the stated reason that carbohydrate is least time-variable then, but manipulates the sink by FRUIT REMOVAL at constant 25 degC day and night, not by temperature; (b) 925 manipulates night temperature properly (-1, 4, 9 degC) and measures leaf glucose and fructose, but reports no time of day for sampling and co-varies day temperature (11/16/21 degC). 874 has the same design gap in the heat direction. 1246 asserts the C3 direction (A2-017) but only as a review sentence citing Qi et al. 2011, with no compartment, sampling time, or magnitude. Corpus-wide regexes for '(pre-)dawn|end of the night|end of the dark period' near a sugar term, and for 'night temperature' near 'starch|hexose|glucose|fructose', returned nothing better than what is cited here.

THE C3 TENSION, BOTH SIDES, HONESTLY. Route 1 (cool night -> less sink consumption -> MORE dawn sugar) is supported by A2-016 (low temperature -> non-structural carbohydrate accumulation in tomato leaves), A2-017 (low night temperature -> higher soluble sugars and starch), A2-018 (sink restriction -> less overnight starch export), A2-019 (sink strength decline -> reduced export -> leaf starch accumulation), A2-022 and A2-023 (independent cucumber reports of large morning starch and total sugar rises on sink removal), and the model chain A2-014/A2-035/A2-036 which makes cool-night residual non-structural carbohydrate a definitional consequence. Route 2 (cool night -> LESS dawn sugar, or no change) is supported by A2-020 (the single best-designed test - sink demand removed, sugars measured at end of night - null), A2-028 (leaf fructose significantly LOWER under both low-temperature regimes than at optimal), A2-029 (authors explicitly report their crop result diverges from the Arabidopsis cold-sugar literature; glucose not significantly different between treatments), A2-030 (proposed mechanism of increased hexose CONSUMPTION under cold), and A2-033 (in Arabidopsis, glucose specifically declines steadily from day 4 of sustained cold while fructose and sucrose stay flat). Note that A2-020 and A2-022 are the same species, same manipulation and same time of day and disagree; this is a real unresolved conflict, not a resolvable one.

CONFOUNDS THE DOWNSTREAM ROLES SHOULD CARRY. (i) Direction is not specific to cooling: A2-019 and A2-037 both show leaf hexose/starch rising at SUPRA-optimal temperature, so 'elevated leaf hexose' does not identify a cool night. (ii) An active-production route exists: A2-031 and A2-032 show cold induces osmoprotective sugar accumulation and vacuolar invertase-driven sucrose-to-hexose hydrolysis, so any cold-associated hexose rise need not come from failed structural conversion. (iii) Compartment is unresolved everywhere: every measurement I found is a whole-leaf destructive extract; nothing distinguishes apoplast, symplast, vacuole or guard cell, and A2-032 places the cold-induced hexose production in the vacuole specifically. (iv) DIF evidence (A2-006) runs against the naive C2 premise - at equal 24-h mean, a COOLER night gives MORE stem elongation. (v) A2-005 and A2-012 are nulls: for a mature crop, the 24-h mean rather than the day/night split governs growth, and 18-24 degC does not directly change partitioning. (vi) A2-013 separates rate from efficiency: the conversion coefficient from assimilate to structural dry matter is held to be temperature-independent, so C2 must be read as a rate/sink-activity claim, not an efficiency claim. (vii) A2-024 is the sharpest single result for the whole hypothesis chain: reduced sink activity DID coincide with higher stomatal resistance in cucumber, but with end-of-night leaf sugars flat - the phenomenology without the proposed hexose mediator.
